strengths: Addresses relevant problem of understanding and identifying failure modes in robot policies with clear motivation
Systematic methodology with three clearly defined stages and proper mathematical formulation using MDPs and PPO
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple robot learning models (BC, hierarchical BC, IQL, BC Transformer, BDQL) with different input modalities
Effective multi-faceted visualizations (radar plots, heatmaps, bar charts) that communicate model vulnerabilities clearly
Well-documented appendices with hyperparameters, network architectures, and detailed rationales for design choices
weaknesses: Critical flaw: Core claim that policy output probabilities π_θ(a|o_i) directly translate to calibrated failure probabilities P_failure(a) lacks rigorous validation—no empirical evidence that extracted probabilities correlate with actual failure rates
No baseline comparisons: Missing critical evaluation against random action selection, grid search, or existing failure prediction methods (e.g., [6, 20])
No ablation studies on key design choices: Hand-crafted reward function, discount factor γ, CNN architecture, and PPO algorithm selection are not systematically evaluated
Superficial experimental validation: Results only demonstrate that models overfit (unsurprising finding); no validation that identified failure modes are representative or actionable

Severe scope limitations: Only 3 manipulation tasks with simple color/size perturbations in simulation; acknowledged need to 'dramatically increase action space' suggests framework is severely limited
Limited novelty: Closely parallels existing RL-based failure discovery work [6, 20, 22, 23]; methodological contribution is primarily application to robotics rather than fundamental innovation
Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, error bars, significance testing, or sensitivity analysis; variance and sample sizes not reported

Methodological concerns: Softmax normalization alone does not ensure probability calibration; entropy-robustness relationship mentioned anecdotally without rigorous validation; unclear distinction between 9 'failure modes' and 9 discrete actions
No real robot validation: All evaluation in simplified simulation environments that do not reflect realistic failure modes
Incomplete positioning: Does not clearly differentiate from highly related work [6, 20] that uses similar RL-based approaches for failure discovery in other domains

strengths: Addresses a relevant and important problem of understanding failures in robot learning policies
Reasonable motivation for using RL to systematically explore failure scenarios
Evaluation across multiple robot learning approaches and input modalities
Implementation details and hyperparameters provided for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applies existing RL-based failure discovery techniques to robotics; prior work ([6], [20], [22], [23]) already uses RL for failure discovery in other domains
Unjustified core claim: the jump from π_θ(a|o_i) to P_failure(a) in Equation 7 lacks theoretical justification; these are relative action preferences, not calibrated failure probabilities
Fundamental conceptual error: conflates 'failure modes' (distinct failure categories in reliability engineering) with discrete action indices; misses the semantic meaning of failure modes
Experiments limited to simple simulation-only tasks with trivial perturbations (color/size changes); no real-world validation or sim2real transfer
No demonstration of actionability: identifies failure-prone scenarios but provides no evidence that these insights can improve policies or enhance robustness
No baseline comparisons: lacks comparison to random perturbation, grid search, uncertainty quantification, or other failure detection methods
No ablation studies or sensitivity analyses validating design choices
Unvalidated probability claims: no empirical validation that assigned probabilities are accurate or calibrated against actual failure rates
Scalability concerns: only works with discrete action spaces; unclear how it extends to continuous control or discovers unexpected failure modes
Missing fundamental experiments: no study of sim2real transfer, no retraining validation, no comparison of predicted vs. actual failure rates

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an important practical challenge in safe robot deployment
Clear and well-structured framework with three well-defined components
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models with diverse input modalities
Excellent visualizations (radar plots, heatmaps, bar charts) that effectively communicate results
Detailed appendices with complete hyperparameters, architecture specifications, and mathematical justifications
weaknesses: Core methodological issue: Interpreting RL policy action probabilities π_θ(a|o_i) as failure probabilities is not well-justified—these represent what the agent learned to induce failures, not absolute failure probability estimates
No experimental validation that identified failure modes actually induce failures; lacks quantitative comparison against random sampling or other red-teaming baselines
No ablation studies on critical design choices (reward function design, hyperparameters); single reward function design unjustified
Limited novelty: applying existing RL red-teaming techniques (acknowledged by citations [20], [22], [23]) to robot policies without novel technical contributions
No demonstration of practical utility: the paper identifies failures but provides no mechanism or evidence that these insights can improve policies or real-world deployment
Narrow experimental scope: only simulation, simple manipulation tasks, discrete actions, 6 models, limited perturbation types; authors acknowledge action space too small
No statistical analysis: no confidence intervals, significance tests, multiple runs, or error bars reported
Missing critical evaluations: transferability to real robots, sensitivity to RL optimization, scalability to continuous/high-dimensional perturbations

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical challenges in robot policy robustness
Comprehensive experimental validation across 6+ tasks with both simulation and real robot experiments
Consistent empirical improvements over RL and VLM baselines (82.2% vs 75.0% average score)
Technically sound framework integrating RL, vision-language embeddings, and contrastive learning coherently
Good presentation with clear figures and well-documented algorithms
Addresses both discrete and continuous action spaces, showing generality
Extensive ablations and analysis of learned embeddings
Practical insights from failure mode analysis that could guide policy improvement
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (RL, ViT/CLIP, contrastive learning) without new methodological contributions
VLM baselines appear unfair, as GPT-4o and Gemini were not designed for this task, making the comparison somewhat misleading
Generalization claims are overstated—'unseen environments' remain similar to training scenarios (color/shape variations only), not truly novel settings
Critical practical details missing: computational cost of PPO-based failure discovery, wall-clock time comparisons, and scalability analysis not discussed
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple run reporting; unclear if improvements are statistically significant
Fine-tuning improvements are modest (5-10% in some cases), questionable if added complexity is justified
No comparison with simpler baselines like random environment perturbations or domain randomization
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned, real robot experiments limited to single platform (UR5e)
Limited validation that discovered failure modes align with expert expectations or other external criteria
All experiments on similar tabletop manipulation tasks; scalability to mobile manipulation or fundamentally different domains unclear

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem in robot learning—systematic failure diagnosis is valuable for improving policy robustness
Comprehensive system design that thoughtfully integrates PPO, vision-language embeddings, and continuous action space exploration
Extensive experimental evaluation across multiple tasks, environments, and both simulation and real-world settings
Includes detailed ablation studies on embedding architectures, loss functions, and fine-tuning procedures with good visualizations
Demonstrates real robot applicability (UR5e) and provides analysis of failure mode characteristics across different configurations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (PPO, CLIP embeddings, standard RL) without significant algorithmic innovation or fundamental insights

Weak baseline comparisons: comparing against A2C/SAC (not designed for failure diagnosis) and GPT-4o/Gemini (not designed for robotics) does not validate the approach; missing comparisons against robustness testing and failure analysis methods from verification/robotics literature

Overstated generalization claims: all 21 'unseen environment' variations are minor visual perturbations (colors, lighting, shapes); no evidence of transfer to truly novel domains or significant distribution shifts

Unclear practical impact: connection between identified failures and actual policy improvement is weak; fine-tuning results lack comparison to simpler baselines (domain randomization, adversarial training); no evidence that discovered failures align with user priorities

Methodological concerns: RL reward function (Eq. 2) biases toward easily-triggered failures; assumption that discrete perturbations map to failure-inducing actions lacks validation; many hyperparameter choices lack justification

Evaluation methodology issues: no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals on most results; embedding quality metrics (Fig. 9) show weak diagonal dominance; 'ground truth' failures are not defined or validated

Limited scope and scalability: real experiments restricted to single robot setup and 6 tasks; vision-language embedding training under-described; no analysis of computational costs or scalability to complex environments

Inadequate discussion of limitations: admits VLM performance below 60% without meaningful resolution; no analysis of failure cases; missing guidance on practical application and hyperparameter sensitivity

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated, practically important problem in robotics—systematic failure diagnosis for manipulation policies
Comprehensive framework thoughtfully combining complementary techniques (discrete/continuous RL exploration + vision-language embeddings)
Extensive experimental validation across 6+ tasks in both simulation and real-world settings (UR5e robot)
Strong empirical results showing RoboMD identifies more failures than baselines and can improve policy robustness through targeted fine-tuning
Demonstrates generalization to unseen environment variations, validating robustness of the approach
Technically sound methodology with clear mathematical formulations and reasonable design choices
Well-documented with thorough appendices, detailed experimental setup, and comprehensive ablations
Effective visualizations that clearly communicate framework and results
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—combines existing techniques (PPO, CLIP embeddings, RL) rather than proposing novel methodology
Weak baseline comparisons—VLM baselines not designed for robotic failure analysis; missing comparisons with other interpretability/diagnostic methods in robotics
Insufficient statistical rigor—no error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-run variance analysis reported
Scalability concerns—computational costs not discussed; limited to relatively simple single-arm manipulation tasks; unclear performance on complex multi-step or contact-rich tasks
Generalization limitations—assumes failures can be induced by modefined environmental factors; unclear how method handles failure modes unrelated to these factors
Fine-tuning improvements sometimes modest—e.g., Fig. 14 shows limited gains for certain table colors
Depends heavily on quality of CLIP embeddings—Table V shows inconsistent results (Image+Text sometimes underperforms Image-only) without adequate discussion
Continuous action space embedding approach relies on pre-computed known-failure embeddings, potentially limiting discovery of truly novel failures
Missing code availability statement and limited discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity
Lacks comparison with alternative failure discovery approaches (e.g., curriculum learning, adversarial methods)
